entry: Corps of the French Army open to foreign nationals. King Louis-Philippe founded the Legion on March 10, 1831, to absorb foreigners into French service. It was first stationed in Algeria and later fought in the [[Crimean War]] and the [[Franco-Prussian War]]. Its training stresses traditional military skills and *esprit de corps* among men from many countries, and it is often described as physically challenging and psychologically stressful. Legionnaires may apply for French citizenship after service, or immediately if wounded in the line of duty.

Overseas department and region of France on the northern coast of South America. It is bordered by [[Suriname]] to the west and Brazil to the east and south, and covers 84,000 sq km (32,000 sq mi). The population was 298,554 as of January 2026, with 3.88 inhabitants per sq km, and about half of residents live in the capital, Cayenne. Approximately 98.9% of the territory is forested, much of it primeval [[Rainforest|rainforest]], and Guiana Amazonian Park covers 41% of it. The Guiana Space Centre near the equator is now the primary launch site of the [[European Space Agency]]. Fully integrated into the French Republic since 1946, the territory uses the euro. Standard French is the official language, but French Guianese [[Creole language|Creole]], a French-based creole, is the most widely spoken.

Group of French-dependent territories in Southeast Asia, from 1887 to 1954. It was first a federation of French colonies and from 1949 a confederation of French associated states. It comprised [[Cambodia]], [[Laos]], the Chinese territory of Guangzhouwan (1898–1945), and the Vietnamese regions of Tonkin, Annam and Cochinchina, with [[Hanoi]] and Saigon as capitals. The French drew revenue from monopolies on opium, salt and rice alcohol, and colonial rule provoked sporadic rebellions. Japanese forces overthrew the regime on March 9, 1945. On September 2, 1945, [[Ho Chi Minh]] proclaimed the independence of the Democratic Republic of Vietnam, and French efforts to regain control led to the [[First Indochina War]]. Defeat at Điện Biên Phủ and the Geneva Accords of July 21, 1954, ended French Indochina, though Laos and Cambodia had gained independence in 1953.

Overseas collectivity of France in the South Pacific Ocean. It comprises 121 islands and atolls spread over more than 2,000 km, with a total land area of 3,521 sq km and a population of 282,596 as of September 2025. The islands form five groups, and [[Tahiti]], the most populous, was home to nearly 69% of residents in 2017. Papeete, on Tahiti, is the capital. European contact began in 1521, when [[Ferdinand Magellan]] sighted Puka-Puka. The French took over in 1842 and established a protectorate, which became an overseas territory in 1946 and was renamed French Polynesia in 1957. Since 2003 it has been an overseas collectivity, and the [[United Nations]] classifies it as a non-self-governing territory.

Series of military conflicts from 1792 to 1802 arising from the [[French Revolution]], in which [[France]] fought Great Britain, Austria, Prussia, Russia and other states. They comprised the War of the First Coalition (1792–1797) and the War of the Second Coalition (1798–1802). After France declared war on Austria and Prussia in spring 1792, a coordinated invasion was turned back at Valmy in September. Mass [[Conscription|conscription]] sustained the army, which conquered the Low Countries and the Rhineland. In 1796 [[Napoleon|Napoleon Bonaparte]] began a campaign in Italy that led to the Treaty of Campo Formio on October 17, 1797. The Second Coalition began in 1798 with Napoleon's invasion of Egypt. After victories at Marengo and Hohenlinden, Austria sought peace, and Britain signed the Treaty of Amiens in 1802.

Series of civil wars between French Catholics and Protestants, called Huguenots, from 1562 to 1598. Between two and four million people died from violence, famine or disease caused by the conflict, which severely damaged the power of the French monarchy. Both sides received foreign support, with Spain and Savoy backing the Catholics and England and the Dutch Republic the Protestants. [[Catherine de' Medici]] initially backed moderates but later supported the St. Bartholomew's Day massacre of 1572, in which Catholic mobs killed between 5,000 and 30,000 Protestants throughout France. The wars ended with the Edict of Nantes, issued in 1598 by [[Henry IV of France|Henry IV]], who had converted to Catholicism in 1593. Catholic opposition persisted, and [[Louis XIV]] revoked the edict in 1685.

North American theater of the [[Seven Years' War]], fought from 1754 to 1763 between Great Britain and France with their Indigenous allies. Historians generally treat it as part of the global Seven Years' War, but in the United States it is often viewed as a distinct conflict. It began in May 1754 at the Battle of Jumonville Glen, when Virginia militia led by [[George Washington]] ambushed a French patrol. Edward Braddock's expedition was defeated at the Battle of the Monongahela in 1755, and Britain captured [[Quebec]] in 1759 and Montreal the following year. The Treaty of Paris in 1763 transferred France's Canadian possessions and its claims east of the [[Mississippi River]] to Britain. Spain received French Louisiana west of the river, and France retained only [[Saint Pierre and Miquelon]].

Overseas colonies, protectorates and mandate territories ruled by France. A first empire, which existed until 1814 and lost most of its holdings, was followed by a second that began with the conquest of [[Algiers]] in 1830. On the eve of [[World War I]], France's empire was the second-largest after the British Empire. Losses in the [[Seven Years' War]] removed most of its North American possessions, and Louisiana, returned to France in 1800, was sold to the United States in 1803. After the [[Franco-Prussian War]], colonies seemed a way to restore French prestige, and the empire was rebuilt mostly after 1850 in Africa, Indochina and the South Pacific. Its ideology, the *mission civilisatrice*, promised French language and institutions, but colonial subjects were rarely granted full citizenship. [[Charles de Gaulle]] and the Free French used the colonies as a base in [[World War II]]. Revolts in Indochina and Algeria cost France both colonies after 1945.

Cooking traditions and practices of France. In the 14th century the court chef Guillaume Tirel, known as "Taillevent," wrote *Le Viandier*, one of the earliest recipe collections of medieval France. In the 17th and 18th centuries, chefs François Pierre La Varenne and Marie-Antoine Carême led a shift away from foreign influences, such as [[Italian cuisine|Italian]] cooking, toward a distinctly French style. Cheese and wine are central, with regional variations governed by *appellation d'origine contrôlée* (AOC) laws. From the 20th century, culinary tourism and the Guide Michelin helped commoners discover urban *cuisine bourgeoise* and peasant cooking. In November 2010 [[UNESCO]] added French gastronomy to its lists of intangible cultural heritage.

Batonnet or julienne-cut potato strips, deep-fried until crisp, of disputed origin. The potatoes are cut into even strips, dried and fried in two stages: the first bath, at about 160 °C (320 °F), cooks them through, and a briefer fry at 190 °C (375 °F) crisps the outside. They are typically salted and served with ketchup, mustard, vinegar or mayonnaise. Since the 1960s, most American fries have been made from frozen [[Potato|russet potatoes]]. [[McDonald's]] used a blend of 93% beef tallow and 7% cottonseed oil until 1990, then switched to vegetable oil with beef flavoring.

Napoleon's 1812 offensive against the [[Russian Empire]], launched to force Russia to comply with the continental blockade of the United Kingdom. The campaign began on June 24, 1812, when the multinational Grande Armée crossed the Neman River with nearly half a million men. Napoleon captured Smolensk in August after a two-day battle, but the Russian army avoided encirclement and kept retreating. At Borodino he failed to destroy it, and on September 14 he entered [[Moscow]], which had been abandoned and set ablaze. Waiting there for a peace that never came, he began a retreat in October. Hunger, cold, [[Typhus]] and attacks by [[Cossacks|Cossacks]] devastated the army. Around a million soldiers and civilians died in less than six months, and the campaign shattered Napoleon's reputation for invincibility.

Literature written in the French language, particularly by French citizens. Works by writers from Belgium, Switzerland, Canada and African countries are termed Francophone literature. One of the first known examples is the *Song of Roland*, a *chanson de geste*. From the 11th century, medieval French literature was one of the oldest vernacular literatures in western Europe, and in the 17th century French letters dominated Europe. In the 18th century French became the literary [[Lingua franca|lingua franca]] and diplomatic language of western Europe. France ranks first among countries for [[Nobel Prize|Nobel Prizes]] in literature, and as of 2022 fifteen French authors had won the prize. [[Jean-Paul Sartre]] declined the 1964 award, arguing that a writer must not be turned into an institution.

Number of occurrences of a repeating event per unit of time. Frequency specifies the rate of oscillations and vibrations in science and engineering, including sound, radio waves and light. The period, the time between events, is its reciprocal: a heart beating 120 times per minute (2 [[Hertz|hertz]]) has a period of half a second. The SI unit is the hertz (Hz), named after the German physicist [[Heinrich Hertz]] by the International Electrotechnical Commission in 1930 and adopted by the General Conference on Weights and Measures in 1960. Sixty revolutions per minute equals one hertz. Angular frequency, measured in radians per second, is frequency multiplied by 2π.

City (pop., 2020: 542,107) in the San Joaquin Valley of [[California]], county seat of Fresno County. It is the most populous city in Central California and the largest in the Central Valley region, and it ranks as the fifth-most populous city in California. Founded in 1872 as a station on the Central Pacific Railroad, it was incorporated in 1885. Its name, Spanish for ash tree, refers to the trees lining the San Joaquin River. Agriculture dominates the surrounding economy, and [[Yosemite National Park]] lies about 60 miles (100 km) to the north.

Norse goddess associated with love, beauty, fertility, war, gold and *seiðr*, a form of magic for seeing and influencing the future. She owns the necklace Brísingamen, rides a chariot drawn by two cats, and has a cloak of falcon feathers that lets her shift into falcon form. A member of the Vanir, she is the mother of Hnoss and Gersemi by her husband Óðr, who is often absent, and she weeps tears of red gold for him. Freyja receives half of those slain in battle at her hall Fólkvangr, while the other half go to [[Odin]]'s hall, Valhalla. She is attested in the [[Poetic Edda]] and in the Prose Edda and *Heimskringla* by [[Snorri Sturluson]], and her name survives in several plant names in southern Sweden.

Force resisting the relative motion of solid surfaces, fluid layers and other materials sliding or grinding against each other. Types include dry, fluid, lubricated, skin and internal friction. Dry friction arises mainly from surface irregularities called asperities and is divided into static friction between non-moving surfaces and kinetic friction between moving ones. The study of friction, called tribology, has a history of more than 2,000 years. Ancient writers including [[Aristotle]] were interested in its causes, and [[Leonardo da Vinci]] discovered the classic laws of sliding friction in 1493. His notebooks were not published, and Guillaume Amontons rediscovered the laws in 1699. Friction can start fires, as rubbing wood together shows, and its wear degrades performance and damages components.

Mexican painter known for autobiographical self-portraits and works drawing on Mexican folk art. Born to a German father and a mestiza mother, she spent most of her life at La Casa Azul, the family home in Coyoacán. Polio in 1913 and a bus accident at age 18 left her with chronic pain, which became a frequent subject of her paintings. She joined the Mexican Communist Party in 1927 and married [[Diego Rivera]] in 1929. Surrealist André Breton arranged her first solo exhibition, at the Julien Levy Gallery in New York in 1938. The [[Louvre]] bought *The Frame*, making her the first Mexican artist in its collection. Her work was rediscovered in the late 1970s, and by the early 1990s she was an icon for Chicanos, feminists and the LGBTQ+ community. Her 1940 self-portrait *The Dream (The Bed)* holds the record for the most expensive work by a female artist ever auctioned, at $54.7 million.

Day of the week between Thursday and Saturday. It is the fifth day of the week under the Monday-first convention and the sixth under Sunday-first. In most Western countries it is the last day of the working week, while in Iran it ends the weekend. The English name derives from Old English *frīġedæġ*, meaning day of Frig, reflecting a convention that linked the Germanic goddess Frigg with the Roman goddess Venus. Most [[Romance languages|Romance languages]] derive the name from Latin *dies Veneris*, or day of Venus. In Arabic it is *al-jumʿah*, meaning congregation.

Norwegian polymath, explorer and diplomat. In 1888 Nansen led the first crossing of [[Greenland]] interior on cross-country skis. His 1893–1896 *Fram* expedition reached a record northern latitude of 86°14′, and his polar travel techniques influenced later [[Arctic]] and Antarctic expeditions. He studied [[Zoology|zoology]], and his doctoral research on the central nervous system of marine creatures helped establish the neuron doctrine. He then turned to oceanography, making many cruises mainly in the North Atlantic. In 1905 he spoke for ending Norway's union with Sweden and persuaded Prince Carl of Denmark to accept the Norwegian throne. Appointed in 1921 as the [[League of Nations]]' High Commissioner for Refugees, he introduced the "Nansen passport" for stateless people, which more than 50 countries recognized. He received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1922.

German philosopher, social theorist and revolutionary socialist. Engels collaborated with [[Karl Marx]] for life, co-authoring *The Communist Manifesto* in 1848 and helping develop what became [[Marxism]]. Born into a prosperous mercantile family in Barmen, Prussia, he was sent to Manchester, England, in 1842 to work in a family cotton mill. His observations there informed *The Condition of the Working Class in England* (1845). He fought in the [[Revolutions of 1848]] before going into exile in England. For two decades he worked for the family firm of Ermen & Engels while supporting the impoverished Marx family in London. After Marx's death in 1883 he edited the second and third volumes of *Das Kapital*. He died in London in 1895.

Austrian economist and political philosopher. He studied at the [[University of Vienna]], earning doctorates in law in 1921 and political studies in 1923, and as a teenager he fought in [[World War I]]. Hayek became a British national in 1938 and taught at the [[London School of Economics]] and later the [[University of Chicago]]. He was a notable member of the Austrian school of economics. He shared the 1974 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences with Gunnar Myrdal for work on money and economic fluctuations. His most popular work, *The Road to Serfdom* (1944), has been republished many times. Although sometimes called a conservative, he preferred the labels classical liberal or libertarian. He received the Presidential Medal of Freedom from [[George H. W. Bush]] in 1991.

German economist and political theorist. Born in Reutlingen, he was appointed professor of public administration at Tübingen in 1817 despite lacking a university degree. He developed a nationalist theory of political economy in Europe and the [[United States]], and he argued for the Zollverein, a pan-German customs union. List advocated tariffs on imported goods while supporting free trade within the nation, and he saw the cost of a tariff as an investment in future productivity. He is regarded as a forerunner of the German historical school of economics, and Emmanuel Todd considers him a precursor to [[John Maynard Keynes]] as a theorist of regulated capitalism. His later years were marked by financial failures, and he died by suicide in 1846.

German philosopher and classical philologist. In 1869, at age 24, he became professor of classical philology at the University of [[Basel]], but ill health forced him to resign in 1879. He then worked as an independent writer, moving between Switzerland, Italy and southern France. His mature works include *Thus Spoke Zarathustra*, *Beyond Good and Evil* and *On the Genealogy of Morality*. He critiqued objective truth in favor of perspectivism, attacked Christian morality as a slave morality, and developed the concepts of the *Übermensch*, the will to power and eternal return. After a neurological collapse in 1889 he was cared for by his mother and then his sister. Elisabeth Förster-Nietzsche edited his unpublished writings to fit her ultranationalist ideology, and his work became associated with fascism and [[Nazism]]. Twentieth-century scholars such as Walter Kaufmann defended his original views, and his influence spans [[Existentialism|existentialism]] and [[Postmodernism|postmodernism]].

German playwright, poet, philosopher and historian. Considered one of Germany's most important classical playwrights, Schiller was a leading figure of the *Sturm und Drang* movement. Born in Marbach to a Lutheran family, he was first intended for the priesthood, then entered a military academy in [[Stuttgart]] and studied medicine. His first play, *The Robbers*, was highly successful. In 1789 he became professor of history and philosophy at the University of Jena. During the last 17 years of his life he was close to [[Johann Wolfgang von Goethe]], encouraging him to finish works. Together they founded the Weimar Theater and shaped Weimar Classicism, and they worked together on *Xenien*, a collection of satirical poems.

German chemist. He was the first to isolate [[Beryllium]] and [[Yttrium]] in pure metallic form and the first to prepare several inorganic compounds, including silane and silicon nitride. He is credited with the first isolation of aluminum in pure form. In 1828 he synthesized [[Urea|urea]] from inorganic substances, which challenged the vitalist belief that organic compounds arose only in living organisms, although historians debate how far this undermined vitalism. He became professor of chemistry at the [[University of Göttingen|University of Göttingen]] in 1836 and held the chair until his death, 46 years later. Approximately 8,000 research students were trained in his laboratory there. He also worked closely with [[Justus von Liebig]] on the radical theory of organic structure.
